Que la probabilidad continua necesitaba: That continuous probability needed integrals was not obvious. Through the eighteenth century people handled “geometric probabilities” with ad hoc area arguments, and out of that came in 1777 Buffon's needle, which estimates $\pi$ by dropping a needle on a floor of planks. Laplace systematised the calculus with densities, but the rigorous definition of continuous probability had to wait for Lebesgue to rebuild the integral from scratch at the start of the twentieth century and for Kolmogorov, in 1933, to axiomatise the whole of probability in a few pages. That a school student today computes these areas with Barrow's rule is the result of two hundred years of clarifying exactly what was being done.
